title: Finite Automata & Regular Languages
summary: DFAs, NFAs, their equivalence, and regular expressions — grounds why regex can't match balanced parentheses.

slides.markdown:
A **formal language** is just a set of strings over some fixed **alphabet** (a set of symbols). `{0,1}*` binary strings, valid email addresses, valid Python identifiers — each is a language.

**Finite automata** are the simplest machines that can recognize (accept/reject) a language — no memory beyond "which state am I in."

- **Alphabet** — the symbols allowed (e.g. `{a,b}`).
- **String** — a finite sequence of alphabet symbols.
- **Language** — the set of strings a machine accepts.
- Regular languages are exactly what a finite automaton can recognize — no more, no less.

slides.subTitle: States and transitions
slides.markdown:
A **DFA** is states plus transitions: from each state, exactly one transition per input symbol. Start in the start state, follow transitions as you read input, accept if you end in an **accepting state**.

![A DFA's states, transitions, start, and accepting state](assets/dfa-states-transitions.svg)

"Deterministic" means no choice — the next state is fully determined by the current state and symbol.

assets.alt: A DFA's states, transitions, start, and accepting state

slides.subTitle: The intuition of "guessing"
slides.markdown:
An **NFA** relaxes the one-transition-per-symbol rule: a state can have zero, one, or multiple transitions for the same symbol, plus **ε-transitions** (moves that consume no input).

The intuition: an NFA "guesses" the right path and accepts if *any* path reaches an accepting state. You can picture it as exploring all possible paths in parallel and succeeding if one of them works.

This makes NFAs much easier to *design* for some patterns (e.g. "contains `ab` somewhere") even though they don't recognize any language a DFA couldn't.

slides.subTitle: NFA-to-DFA equivalence
slides.markdown:
The **subset construction** converts any NFA into an equivalent DFA: each DFA state represents *the set of all NFA states reachable so far*. Since there are only finitely many subsets of a finite state set, this always terminates in a valid (if sometimes larger) DFA.

This proves NFAs and DFAs recognize exactly the same class of languages — NFAs add **convenience**, not **power**. Anything an NFA can do, a DFA (potentially with exponentially more states) can do too.

This is why regex engines can always compile down to a deterministic matcher, even when written non-deterministically.

slides.subTitle: Kleene's theorem
slides.markdown:
**Kleene's theorem** says regular expressions and finite automata define exactly the same class of languages: every regex has an equivalent NFA, and every finite automaton has an equivalent regex.

This is why regex libraries can compile a pattern into a state machine under the hood — `a*b+` isn't just notation, it's literally describing a specific automaton's structure.

"Regular" as a term comes from this equivalence: a language is **regular** exactly when some finite automaton (equivalently, some regex) can recognize it.

slides.subTitle: Building a DFA for a concrete pattern
slides.markdown:
DFA for "binary strings ending in `01`" over `{0,1}`:

```
states: q0 (start), q1, q2 (accept)
q0 --0--> q1     q0 --1--> q0
q1 --0--> q1     q1 --1--> q2
q2 --0--> q1     q2 --1--> q0
```

Trace `1101`: `q0 -1-> q0 -1-> q0 -0-> q1 -1-> q2`. Ends in `q2` (accept) — correct, since the string ends in `01`.

slides.subTitle: The pumping lemma
slides.markdown:
The **pumping lemma** says: for any regular language, strings longer than some length `p` must contain a repeatable middle segment — you can "pump" (repeat) it any number of times and the result stays in the language.

To prove a language is **not** regular, assume it is, then show a long enough string where *no* such repeatable segment works — every possible split leads to a contradiction (some pumped version leaves the language).

It's a proof-by-contradiction template: assume regularity, derive an impossible consequence, conclude the language isn't regular.

slides.subTitle: Balanced parentheses isn't regular
slides.markdown:
Regex famously can't fully match balanced, arbitrarily-nested parentheses like `(()(()))`. Here's why: a DFA has only **finitely many states**, so it can only "remember" a bounded amount of nesting depth. Beyond that many opens, it runs out of distinct states to track how deep it is.

Applying the pumping lemma to `{(ⁿ)ⁿ}` confirms this rigorously — no finite automaton can recognize it.

This is exactly why real parsers use a **stack** (pushdown automata / context-free grammars), which have unbounded memory for nesting — regex alone is the wrong tool for nested structure.

Finite automata aren't just theory — they're the engine behind everyday tools. A compiler's **lexer** tokenizes source code by running regex-equivalent DFAs over the character stream (Area 6 `compilers`). Form validation ("is this a valid phone number/email") is regex, i.e. a finite automaton, checking membership in a regular language.

The practical takeaway: whenever you reach for regex, you're implicitly betting the pattern has no unbounded nested structure — which is true for tokens and simple formats, but not for parsing code or matched brackets.
